questions.q: What are the four native Salesforce report format types?
options: Tabular, Summary, Matrix, and Joined
Pie, Bar, Line, and Funnel
Standard, Custom, Historical, and Snapshot
Public, Private, Shared, and Locked
questions.explain: Salesforce reports come in four formats — Tabular (a simple list), Summary (grouped with subtotals), Matrix (grouped by rows and columns), and Joined (multiple report blocks side by side).

questions.q: What is a key limitation of a Tabular report that a Summary report doesn't share?
options: Tabular reports cannot have any filters applied
A Tabular report is just a flat list of records with no grouping, and it can't be used as the source for most dashboard chart components
Tabular reports can only show 5 rows maximum
Tabular reports cannot be exported to Excel
questions.explain: Tabular reports have no grouping or subtotals, which makes them great for simple record lists but unusable for most chart-based dashboard components, which generally need at least one grouping level to chart against.

questions.q: What distinguishes a Matrix report from a Summary report?
options: Summary reports allow unlimited columns of grouping while Matrix reports allow none
Matrix reports cannot include subtotals
Matrix reports group and summarize data by both rows and columns simultaneously, while Summary reports only group by rows (or one dimension)
There is no real difference between them
questions.explain: A Matrix report lets you cross-tabulate data — for example, Opportunity Amount summarized by both Sales Rep (rows) and Close Month (columns) — whereas a Summary report only groups along one primary dimension.

questions.q: What does filter logic (e.g., 1 AND (2 OR 3)) let you do in a Salesforce report that simply stacking filters cannot?
options: Change the report's format from Summary to Matrix
Automatically email the report on a schedule
Add a chart to the report
Combine multiple filter conditions with custom AND/OR relationships instead of always ANDing every filter together
questions.explain: By default, multiple report filters are combined with AND; filter logic lets you reference filter numbers and mix AND/OR (and NOT) to express conditions like 'Stage is Closed Won OR (Amount > 50000 AND Region = West)'.

questions.q: What does a cross filter let you do that a standard field filter cannot?
options: Filter the primary object based on the presence or absence of related child records, using WITH or WITHOUT
Sort results by multiple columns at once
Convert a Tabular report into a Matrix report
Apply a filter only to chart components, not the report itself
questions.explain: A cross filter answers relationship-based questions a field filter can't, like 'show me Accounts WITHOUT any related Opportunities' — filtering based on whether related records exist, not on a field's value.

questions.q: What is bucketing used for in a Salesforce report?
options: Permanently deleting outlier records from the dataset
Grouping a range of field values into custom categories (like 'Small', 'Medium', 'Large' deal sizes) directly in the report, without creating a new formula field
Encrypting sensitive numeric fields
Merging two separate reports into one
questions.explain: Bucketing lets an analyst define ad hoc groupings on the fly (e.g., Amount ranges) inside the report builder itself, which is faster than creating and maintaining a dedicated custom formula field for a one-off grouping need.

questions.q: What is a summary formula in a Salesforce report used for?
options: Calculating a value per individual row, such as a per-row percentage
Renaming report columns
Performing a calculation across a group, subtotal, or the grand total — for example, showing each rep's Amount as a percentage of the grand total
Changing which object the report is built on
questions.explain: Summary formulas operate at the group or grand-total level, aggregating across the rows in that group — ideal for things like 'percent of total' or 'average deal size per rep' that only make sense once rows are combined.

questions.q: How does a row-level formula differ from a summary formula in a report?
options: A row-level formula can only reference other formulas, never real fields
Row-level formulas are only available in Matrix reports
There is no functional difference between row-level and summary formulas
A row-level formula calculates a new value independently for each individual record row, evaluated before any grouping or summarizing happens
questions.explain: Row-level formulas compute a value per record — like flagging whether a single Opportunity's Amount exceeds a threshold — independent of any grouping, unlike summary formulas which need aggregated group data to operate on.

questions.q: What is required before you can add a chart to a Salesforce report?
options: The report must be a Summary or Matrix report with at least one grouping, since charts are built from grouped/summarized data
The report must be shared with every user in the org
The report must be scheduled to run daily
Charts can be added to any report format, including Tabular, with no restrictions
questions.explain: Report charts visualize grouped data, so they require a Summary or Matrix report with at least one grouping level — a flat Tabular report has nothing for the chart to group or plot by.

questions.q: When would a line chart be a better choice than a pie chart for a report on monthly Opportunity revenue?
options: Pie charts should always be used for any numeric data regardless of context
A line chart is better for showing a trend over a continuous sequence like time, while a pie chart is better for showing proportional share of a whole at a single point in time
Line charts cannot display more than one data series, ever
There's no difference — either chart type conveys the same information equally well
questions.explain: Line charts are built for showing change across an ordered sequence (like months), making trend direction visible, while pie charts are meant to show how parts make up a whole at one moment — using a pie chart for a 12-month trend would obscure the trend.

questions.q: What must every Salesforce dashboard component be built from?
options: A raw SOQL query written directly into the dashboard
A Data Loader export file
A source report whose data (and format/grouping) drives what the component can display
An Apex trigger
questions.explain: Each dashboard component (chart, gauge, metric, table) is tied to an underlying report — the dashboard visualizes that report's grouped data, so the report's structure limits what the component can show.

questions.q: What does a dashboard filter let a viewer do that they couldn't do by editing the underlying reports directly?
options: Delete the underlying source reports
Change which users can view the dashboard
Convert dashboard components into report formulas
Interactively narrow down what's shown across multiple dashboard components at once, without needing edit access to any of the underlying reports
questions.explain: Dashboard filters apply on top of the existing components, letting a viewer (with only view access) slice by something like Region or Fiscal Quarter across the whole dashboard at once, without touching the source reports.

questions.q: What's the point of a Dynamic Dashboard that 'runs as' the logged-in user, rather than a fixed running user?
options: Each viewer sees only the data they personally have access to, based on their own sharing and permissions, rather than everyone seeing the fixed running user's view
It makes the dashboard load faster than a static one
It disables all filters on the dashboard
It automatically emails the dashboard to the running user every morning
questions.explain: A dashboard set to run as the logged-in user respects each individual viewer's record-level access — a rep sees only their own deals, while their manager sees their team's — instead of everyone seeing exactly what one fixed running user could see.

questions.q: In sales pipeline analysis, what does 'weighted pipeline' typically refer to?
options: The total count of all open Opportunities regardless of value
The sum of Opportunity Amounts multiplied by each Opportunity's stage-based probability of closing
The average deal size across all closed deals
The number of Opportunities owned by a single sales rep
questions.explain: Weighted pipeline discounts each open Opportunity's Amount by its Probability field (often tied to Stage), giving a more realistic forecast figure than simply summing every open deal at full value.

questions.q: Why do forecast reports typically rely on the Close Date and Stage fields on Opportunities?
options: Because those are the only two fields Salesforce allows on any report
Because Stage and Close Date are automatically deleted after a deal closes
Because Close Date and Stage are used to predict which deals are likely to close and in what period, feeding into forecast categories like Best Case, Commit, and Closed
Because forecasting requires ignoring the Amount field entirely
questions.explain: Forecasting in Salesforce groups Opportunities into forecast categories derived from Stage, and Close Date determines which forecast period (month/quarter) a deal's Amount counts toward — the two fields together drive the whole forecast rollup.

questions.q: What does win/loss analysis on Opportunities primarily help an organization understand?
options: Which users have logged into Salesforce most recently
How many custom fields exist on the Opportunity object
The org's total number of active user licenses
The patterns behind why deals are marked Closed Won versus Closed Lost, such as by competitor, loss reason, or deal size
questions.explain: Win/loss analysis looks at closed Opportunities' outcomes alongside fields like Loss Reason or Competitor to surface patterns — for example, that deals lost to a specific competitor cluster in a certain price range.

questions.q: What is a common metric tracked in Case analytics for a support team?
options: Average time-to-resolution and case volume by priority, channel, or agent
The dollar value of Opportunities closed that quarter
The number of Leads converted from a specific Campaign
The org's API request limit usage
questions.explain: Service Cloud analytics typically centers on operational metrics like average resolution time, case volume trends, and backlog by priority or agent — these tie directly to service-level commitments.

questions.q: How is Campaign ROI typically calculated using Salesforce reporting?
options: By counting how many emails were sent, with no reference to cost or outcome
By comparing the pipeline or revenue generated from Opportunities linked to a Campaign against that Campaign's actual cost
By measuring how many custom fields exist on the Campaign object
ROI cannot be calculated in Salesforce and requires exporting to a separate tool
questions.explain: Campaign ROI reporting weighs the actual cost entered on the Campaign against the revenue or pipeline from Opportunities where that Campaign is marked as a primary campaign source, giving a real return figure.

questions.q: Which of these is a genuine limitation of native Salesforce reporting that often pushes teams toward an external BI tool?
options: Native reports can only ever show a single number with no grouping at all
Native reports cannot be filtered by date

Native reporting has fewer options for advanced statistical modeling, complex cross-object blending beyond a few related objects, and highly customized visual design compared to a dedicated BI/analytics platform
Native reports are only visible to System Administrators
questions.explain: Salesforce's native reports are strong for operational reporting on Salesforce data itself, but they're not built for predictive statistics, blending many disparate data sources, or highly customized visualizations — that's where CRM Analytics or an external BI tool comes in.

questions.q: A team wants one dashboard showing sales pipeline by stage, a service case backlog by priority, and lets each regional VP filter to just their region. What's the right combination of native Salesforce tools to build this?
options: A single Tabular report with no grouping and no dashboard
A single Joined report exported to Excel and emailed manually each week
It cannot be done without CRM Analytics
Summary or Matrix reports (one per topic) as dashboard component sources, assembled on one dashboard with a dashboard filter for Region
questions.explain: This is standard native dashboard construction: build a properly grouped Summary/Matrix report behind each component (pipeline by stage, cases by priority), combine them on one dashboard, and add a dashboard filter on Region so each viewer can narrow the view themselves.
